name: Self-Driving Laboratories
title: Self-Driving Laboratories
answer: Self-driving laboratories are research facilities where software plans experiments, robotic hardware runs them, and instruments measure the results, with the loop repeating without a person at every step. The scope covers the full cycle from choosing a candidate molecule or material to recording the outcome and deciding what to try next. It sits between laboratory automation, which handles the physical execution, and simulation, which predicts results before anything is mixed or heated. Work in this area spans chemistry, materials science, biology and drug discovery, and it is studied as a systems problem rather than a single instrument.

sections.body: Self-driving laboratories are research facilities where software plans experiments, robotic hardware runs them, and instruments measure the results, with the loop repeating without a person at every step. The scope covers the full cycle from choosing a candidate molecule or material to recording the outcome and deciding what to try next. It sits between laboratory automation, which handles the physical execution, and simulation, which predicts results before anything is mixed or heated. Work in this area spans chemistry, materials science, biology and drug discovery, and it is studied as a systems problem rather than a single instrument.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A self-driving lab runs on three layers that have to stay in sync. The physical layer is robotic liquid handlers, plate readers, furnaces, chromatographs and similar instruments, often drawn from commercial laboratory automation lines. The control layer is scheduling and orchestration software that queues jobs, tracks samples and recovers from failures. The decision layer is where models and search algorithms propose the next experiment, and it depends on a database that records every run in a machine readable form. Simulation is frequently used alongside the bench work to screen candidates cheaply before they are made.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done as a closed loop. A model or search strategy proposes a batch of experiments, the scheduler translates that into instrument commands, and the hardware executes them. Results are parsed back into the database, the model is updated, and the next batch is chosen. Because each cycle is slow and expensive, much of the method is about choosing batches that balance exploring unfamiliar regions against refining what already looks promising. Reproducibility depends on capturing conditions, calibration and raw outputs, not just the final number.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this field turn on data provenance, safety and attribution. Every experiment should be traceable to the instrument, the protocol version and the operator or agent that requested it, which is why this site links to original papers rather than to a search tool. Hazardous chemistry, biological material and controlled substances bring regulatory obligations that vary by country and institution. Automated systems can also generate results faster than they can be checked, so review, logging and the handling of failed or anomalous runs matter as much as the science. Questions of who owns machine generated experimental data and who is credited for a discovery remain unsettled.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward tighter integration between simulation and bench work, so that models are trained on data the lab itself produces and the loop closes faster. Standards for describing experiments and instrument interfaces are maturing, which makes it easier to move a protocol between sites. More of the effort is going into making these systems robust over long runs and honest about uncertainty, since a lab that reports confident nonsense is worse than a slow one. The open questions are less about whether the loop can be built and more about how far it can be trusted without a human checking each step.
